answer.label: Not Sun Tzu — from James Clavell's foreword
answer.authorDates: 1921–1994 · Novelist & screenwriter; editor of the 1983 Art of War
answer.sourceLine: The line is not in The Art of War. It appears nowhere in Lionel Giles’s translation or any other, and Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” ↗. Its documented source is the last line of James Clavell’s foreword to his 1983 edition — which reads “the true object of war is peace,” not “objective.” Clavell put it in quotation marks as an old saying (“since ancient times, it has been known that…”) and never credited Sun Tzu, so even Clavell is the vector, not provably the originator.
answer.confidenceText: Confirmed absent from Sun Tzu's text; the Clavell foreword was read directly.

source.excerpt:
Always remember, since ancient times, it has been known that… “the true object of war is peace.”

JAMES CLAVELL
trail: The anchor. Wikiquote’s Sun Tzu page ↗ places “The true objective of war is peace” in its Misattributed section and identifies Clavell’s foreword as the source, noting his wording is “object.” Quote Investigator has no article on this phrase.

The artifact, read directly. The full text of Clavell’s edition ↗ confirms it: the words “object of war is peace” occur at exactly one point in the entire book — the foreword’s last line. The copyright page reads “Copyright © 1983 by James Clavell.”

The negative check. Searching Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation ↗ — the version Clavell adapted — returns nothing for “object of war” or “objective of war.” The closest genuine passage is Chapter II’s warning that no country ever benefited from prolonged warfare.

An earlier echo. Wikiquote also records ↗ Dr. Hiroshi Hatanaka of Kobe College saying “the real objective of war is peace” in Pacific Stars and Stripes, Ryukyu Edition (10 February 1949) — 34 years before Clavell, and not credited to Sun Tzu. We have not examined that issue ourselves; the citation is Wikiquote’s.
source.excerptNote: These are the final words of Clavell’s foreword; the next line on the page is “I. LAYING PLANS — Sun Tzu said…”. Two details do the work: Clavell writes object, not objective, and he sets the line in quotation marks behind “since ancient times, it has been known that…” — presenting it as a saying he is passing along, with no source named and no mention of Sun Tzu.

source.rightsNote: This is a rights question about the foreword, not about Sun Tzu. The Art of War itself is ancient, and Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation is public domain in the US — but this sentence is in neither. The only documented text containing it is James Clavell’s foreword, copyright 1983, which is firmly in copyright. One honest caveat: Clavell quoted the line as a pre-existing saying without naming a source, so the aphorism’s own origin — and therefore its own status — remains undetermined. We make no public-domain claim for a sentence whose origin nobody has traced.

author.name: James Clavell
author.heading: The man whose foreword became a Sun Tzu quote
author.bio: James Clavell was a British-American novelist, screenwriter and director best known for the Asian Saga — King Rat (1962), Tai-Pan (1966), Shōgun (1975) and Noble House (1981). He encountered Sun Tzu in Hong Kong in the 1970s and in 1983 issued his own edition of The Art of War, adapting Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation and adding a fervent foreword urging that the book be made required reading for every officer and politician. That foreword’s closing line is the reason millions of people now believe Sun Tzu wrote a sentence he never wrote.

misattribution.heading: How a foreword became a Sun Tzu quote
misattribution.intro: Three separate things went wrong here — the author, the wording, and the pedigree. Untangling them is what makes this case unusually clear.

items.why: The sentence appears in no translation of The Art of War — not in Giles’s 1910 text ↗, and not in the thirteen chapters of Clavell’s own edition, where the words occur exactly once: in the foreword. Wikiquote lists it under “Misattributed” ↗.

The version in circulation isn’t even the documented sentence. Clavell’s foreword ↗ reads “the true object of war is peace.” The familiar “objective” is a later mutation — a quote misquoting a misattribution.

Clavell is where the line enters wide circulation, but he isn’t proven to have coined it: he set it in quotation marks and introduced it with “since ancient times, it has been known that…”. Wikiquote records the near-identical “the real objective of war is peace” attributed to Dr. Hiroshi Hatanaka in Pacific Stars and Stripes (10 February 1949) — decades before Clavell ↗. We have not independently examined that newspaper.

Clavell’s “ancient times” points West, not East. Aristotle: “we are busy that we may have leisure, and make war that we may live in peace” ↗. Augustine: “it is therefore with the desire for peace that wars are waged” ↗. The thought is genuinely old — just not Chinese, and not Sun Tzu’s.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest summary: an aphorism of unknown origin, quoted without a source by a novelist in a 1983 foreword ↗, mutated by one word in transmission, and then credited to the 2,500-year-old author whose book it introduced.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Sun Tzu is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: any crisp maxim about strategy drifts toward his name, because The Art of War is short, ancient, aphoristic, and exists in dozens of competing translations — which makes any given sentence hard to falsify. If a line sounds like Sun Tzu, it gets to be Sun Tzu.

This one had unusual help. The sentence sits on the last page of Clavell’s foreword, in quotation marks, immediately before Chapter I opens with “Sun Tzu said…”. A reader skimming for a closing line finds a quoted aphorism about war and peace, inches from Sun Tzu’s name, in a book called The Art of War. The misattribution is almost a typographical accident.
context.detailsSummary: What Sun Tzu actually said about ending wars
detailsBody: The sentiment isn’t foreign to Sun Tzu — which is why the fake sticks. Chapter II (“Waging War”) argues that protracted conflict ruins the state: “There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare” ↗, in Giles’s 1910 translation.

But that is an argument for speed, not a teleology of peace. Giles renders the follow-on as: “Only one who knows the disastrous effects of a long war can realize the supreme importance of rapidity in bringing it to a close.” Sun Tzu’s case is economic and prudential — long wars bankrupt you — not the claim that peace is war’s true purpose. The paraphrase upgrades a warning about cost into a moral thesis Sun Tzu never advanced.
context.pull: Clavell wrote “since ancient times, it has been known that…” — an admission that he was quoting someone else. He just never said who.
